column2: Promotion of Improved and Efficient Cooking Practices in the host country of Uganda
column165:
The proposed GS4GG project aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by distributing fuel-efficient Improved Cook Stoves (ICS) to the needy communities of Uganda.
In Uganda, less than 6% of the population has access to clean cooking. Specifically, 11.9% and 3.1% of Uganda's urban and rural residents have access to clean cooking fuels. This accounts for around 95% of households relying on either wood or charcoal as their primary energy source for cooking. Breaking this down further, about 68% of the Ugandan population use firewood as their primary source of cooking fuel, primarily in urban and peri-urban regions. The scenario in rural areas is more devastating, with 85% of the population using firewood as their cooking fuel.  
This heavy dependency on biomass has significantly burdened Uganda's forest, contributing to one of the highest deforestation rates in Sub-saharan Africa. The country's forest cover stands at 11.66%, but it is decreasing at an annual rate of 1.44%. A 2016-2017 National Household Survey found that 63% of firewood users collected the fuel from forests. Moreover, indoor air pollution from biomass use in residential cooking poses a serious health risk, leading to increased air-borne diseases and premature deaths. In 2022, around 3.7 million premature deaths were mainly attributed to household pollution from cooking smoke. While these stoves will significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions, they also provide co-benefits to users.

column2: Improved Cook Stoves VPA-1 (30000 Improved Cooking Stove (ICS) Nepal)
column165:
This Gold Standard (GS) large-scale PoA aims to improve access to clean cooking solutions 
for rural households in Nepal by implementing multiple Voluntary Project Activities (VPAs). 
The PoA will assist households currently using traditional firewood stoves by providing 
better cooking stoves. It will promote one type of clean cook stoves: SSM/S26-11E model 
single pothole rocket stove (SSMRS). The introduction of this project device in the VPAs will reduce firewood consumption and 
lower greenhouse gas emissions that would otherwise be produced.  
The project will contribute to achieving the following Sustainable Development Goals 
(SDGs): SDG 1 (no poverty), SDG 3 (good health and well-being), SDG 4 (quality education), 
SDG 5 (gender equality), SDG 7 (affordable and clean energy), SDG 8 (decent work and 
economic growth), SDG 13 (climate action) and SDG 15 (Life on Land).  
Under the PoA, the project developer aims to implement 100,000 units, contingent on 
funding availability. The project developer will implement the PoA in the physical and 
geographical boundaries of Nepal. The project developer will implement the VPA in the 
physical and geographical boundaries of Bagmati and Gandaki Provinces.

column2: GS12693 VPA- 8 Access to Clean Water in India
column15: ERDA ILLUMINE LOW CARBON SOLUTIONS PRIVATE LIMITED
column165: In 2022, the share of people with a basic access to water resources in India amounted to 93.3% however clean water fit for drinking still remains a challenging aspect. India is ranked 120 out of 122 countries in the global water quality index. Over 75% of households do not have clean drinking water, while 40% of the population will have no access to drinking water by 2030. Waterborne diseases have an economic burden of approximately USD 600 million a year in India. According to WHO diarrhoeal disease is the third leading cause of death in children 1–59 months of age. The project involves water treatment technology for households, that otherwise boil unsafe drinking water using non-renewable sources and/or depend on the consumption of unsafe water (issue of suppressed demand) due to various barrier factors or use energy exhaustive methods to purify water thereby contributing to the emissions by India

column2: GS 23173 VPA-9
column15: ERDA ILLUMINE LOW CARBON SOLUTIONS PRIVATE LIMITED
column165: The VPA aims to provide energy efficient Improved cookstoves (ICS) to the rural communities in the states of West Bengal and Jharkhand in India who rely on traditional firewood cookstove or 3-stone cookstove to cater clean cooking needs at the same time reduce the greenhouse gas emission resulting from inefficient cooking technology. The project involves the distribution of fuel-efficient improved cookstoves (ICS) to replace the baseline traditional cookstoves in rural households. Here ICS refers to both electric cookstove and Improved firewood cookstove together.  3 billion people rely on wood, coal, charcoal for cooking and heating. The Improved cookstoves can reduce the need of wood by 50%. This results in less harmful greenhouse gas emissions and also considerably reduces the pressure on the local forests and biodiversity. The cookstoves generate less smoke and the chimney limits the exposure to smoke to help fight the problem of indoor air pollution and decrease respiratory diseases.

column2: TPREL 460 MW Solar BESS Project in Karnataka
column165:
The purpose of the project is to generate electricity by harnessing the solar energy by using solar photovoltaic technology and there by feed the generated electricity to the Indian national grid. Project involves the installation of 460 MW Solar Photovoltaic Power Plant combined with BESS (115 MWh) in Budgumpi, Karnataka state, India. 
The project is yet to be commissioned and the generated electricity will be supplied to the Indian grid. The power purchase agreement had been signed for the project on 03/05/2024 between Tata Power Renewable Energy Limited (TPREL) and SJVN Limited.

column2: Project Oasis VPA-I
column165: Arukah is scaling a decentralised cow manure-to-biogas model that links carbon credit revenues with direct incentive payments to farmers for verified biogas use. The initiative involves installing household biodigesters and biogas cookstoves that cut greenhouse gas emissions from animal waste management, reduce reliance on firewood and LPG, and improve indoor air quality. Each unit is paired with a continuous stove monitor (CSM) to track real-time biogas production and consumption, ensuring transparent measurement of verified farmer performance. Verified usage is rewarded through digital payouts, establishing a pioneering model of farmer-level carbon-income distribution. Through this approach, Arukah not only supports climate mitigation but also empowers rural households with cleaner energy access, time savings, and integration into formal digital payment and financing systems, advancing both environmental and socioeconomic outcomes.

column2: BaumInvest Flor Saphira Reforestation Project El Capricho & La Catorce
column9: GS Methodology for Afforestation/Reforestation GHG Emissions Reduction and Sequestration
column165:
The "BaumInvest Flor Saphira Reforestation Project El Capricho & La Catorce" is the third Voluntary Project Activity (VPA) in Colombia incorporated into the Programme of Activities (PoA): BaumInvest Forest Landscape Restoration Programme (GS11707). The project focuses on ecological restoration of degraded cattle pastures in the Vichada department, Orinoquia region, municipality of Cumaribo, near the villages of El Capricho and La Catorce.

Key objectives include:

i) Climate change mitigation through long-term carbon sequestration via afforestation.
ii) Sustainable development and poverty alleviation by generating long-term employment in remote, economically underserved areas.
iii) Biodiversity conservation by preserving natural habitats and enhancing habitat connectivity.

This initiative integrates ecological, social, and economic dimensions to advance sustainable land use and restoration.

column2: Global Mangrove Trust Blue Carbon Restoration Project in Indonesia
column165: GMT has initiated a Gold Standard for the Global Goals (GS4GG) Program of Activities (PoA) to support and enable regeneration of degraded mangroves across Indonesia. This country-level PoA, which will cover Indonesia's entire mangrove region, will be executed through several Voluntary Project Activities (VPAs), in partnership with a wide array of stakeholders. GMT is the Coordinating/Managing Entity (CME) for the POA. The project will be carried out by GMT directly,  or in coordination with partner organizations managing the implementation of each VPA. GMT will employ science-based, best practice restoration and monitoring techniques, prioritizing native mangrove species and collaborating closely with local organizations and community groups.

column2: Global Mangrove Trust Blue Carbon Restoration Project in Indonesia - Sumatra 1
column165:
This is a real case VPA-01 under the PoA. This is a transition project from OxCarbon to the Gold Standard for Global Goals. The project under OxCarbon is a community-based conservation and restoration project. The restoration component of the project is being de-registered from OxCarbon and transitioned to GS4GG. 

The CME, GMT, will work with the local NGO, Yayasan Gajah Sumatera (YAGASU) as the VPA Implementer and in association with the local communities. YAGASU, established in 2001, is an Indonesian Foundation having long-term practical experiences on land-based climate actions.  Under this VPA, about 142.82 ha of degraded mangroves will be restored in four villages: Salahaji, Pulau Kampai, Halaban, and Pangkalan Siata in Langkat district, Medan, North Sumatra Province, Indonesia.

Native mangrove species, predominately Rhizophora apiculata, Rhizophora mucronata, Rhizophora stylosa, Ceriops tagal, Bruguiera cylindrica, Bruguiera parviflora and Bruguiera sexangula will be planted on community lands.

column2: Community-based Landscape Restoration in Zambia (COLAREZA)
column165: World Vision Australia (WVA), World Vision Zambia (WVZ) and FORLIANCE intend to implement this Program of Activities with the objective to restore forest landscapes in several regions in Zambia making use of Assisted Natural Regeneration and other forest restoration and management methods. The POA seeks to create and enhance carbon sinks, reduce pressure on woody biomass, restore the local ecology and biodiversity and apply measures of climate smart agriculture whilst delivering significant socio-economic benefits to the local communities. The intent is to develop community-led revegetation projects using primarily Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) on degraded community land to ensure longterm social benefits and carbon removal. FMNR is a low cost, sustainable land restoration technique used to combat poverty and hunger among poor subsistence farmers by increasing food and timber production, and resilience to climate extremes. FMNR promotes the regrowth of indigenous trees, shrubs and naturally occurring seeds in degraded forest and farmland through farmers and community members undertaking selective pruning and protection to encourage the growth of new shoots. Since 2017 the FMNR technique has been promoted by WV'Z to be used by farmers in Miombo forest ecosystems of Zambia. The development of a carbon program is expected to accelerate the adoption of the technique and provide additional incentives for long term sustainability and permanence.

column2: AquaCarbon Safe Water
column9: GS Methodology for emission reductions from safe drinking water supply
column165: The purpose of this PoA is to disseminate low-GHG water purification technologies in Ghana, thereby reducing the need to boil water, which is generally done on unimproved stoves that use firewood and/or charcoal. With only 30% of the population having access to clean cooking fuels and technologies in Ghana,  the project addresses a critical challenge in sustainable water treatment and fuel consumption. The reduction in fossil fuel combustion will lead to a reduction in carbon emissions. The PoA is planned to have a geographical scope expansion in the future.

column2: AquaCarbon Ghana VPA1
column165: The goal of this proposed VPA is the widespread installation of low greenhouse gas (GHG) water purification technologies to community water supply systems for households in northern Ghana to use. Element15 will install and maintain the water treatment systems (BAR systems) at existing water sources situated in rural and peri-urban communities. The BAR systems are based on membrane technology and do not use energy in the filtration process, so the project does not cause greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. This VPA will apply the Gold Standard Methodology "Emission Reductions from Safe Drinking Water Supply" (Version 1.0) to quantify the emission reductions achieved by providing safe drinking water and avoiding the need for water boiling using non-renewable fuel.

column2: Landfill biogas extraction and combustion plant in El Inga I and II landfill (Quito Ecuador)
column9: ACM0001 Flaring or use of landfill gas
column165:
The proposed GS project activity titled "Landfill biogas extraction and combustion plant
in El Inga I and II landfill (Quito, Ecuador)" encompasses collection and
destruction/utilization of landfill gas (LFG) generated at the El Inga I and II landfill. This well-managed landfill is operated by Empresa Pública Metropolitana de Gestión Integral de Residuos Sólidos (EMGIRS) and it is located in Quito, capital city of Ecuador. The El Inga landfill started its Municipal Solid Waste
(MSW) permanent disposal activities in 2003. The project's objective is to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, specifically methane (CH₄), by implementing and operating a highly efficient forced landfill gas
(LFG) collection system. This includes infrastructure for LFG flaring using high temperature enclosed flares, as well as an electricity generation system. The system
consists of seven engine-generator sets, each with a capacity of approximately 1 MW,
fueled exclusively by LFG, resulting in a total combined nameplate power generation
capacity of around 5 MW.

column2: Climate Protection Project in Himalayan Landscape of Uttarakhand
column15: Society for the Upliftment of Villagers and Development of Himalayan Areas (SUVIDHA)
column165:
The Himalayan landscape of Uttarakhand in India is highly vulnerable to climate change impacts  such as forest fires, flash floods, landslides, and changing weather patterns. These issues poses risks to ecosystems, agriculture, infrastructure, and human lives. 

The project aims to mitigate these effects by addressing greenhouse gas emissions, promoting renewable energy while reducing women drudgery in select region.  The project is being implemented in collaboration of Terres des hommes, AMAN, HESCO and SUVIDHA. 

The main objective of this project is to introduce clean and renewable energy technologies viz. biogas plants and smokeless stoves to rural marginal families in four districts of Uttarakhand.  The proposed interventions have the potential to address various socio-economic issues, to upgrade the quality of life in rural areas while also offsetting carbon emissions. The biogas plants and improved cook stoves that are to be promoted under the project will replace energy inefficient methods of cooking thereby leading to improved health and reducing GHG emissions that contribute to climate change.

column2: Mbaula za Makono Banja la thanzi (Improved cookstoves a healthy family) project – Dowa District
column165:
The purpose of this Gold Standard Project is the distribution of fuel-efficient improved cookstoves (ICS) in Malawi. The ICS distributed will replace the existing practices of cooking over an open fire(with an efficiency of 15%), or on low-efficiency traditional cookstoves. The ICS burns non-renewable woody biomass more efficiently, thereby improving thermal energy transfer to pots(thermale efficiency of 30.63% without remaining char and 36.76 with remaining char). Not only shall the envisaged project save fuel wood and reduce greenhouse gases (CO2 and non-CO2), it also creates additional SDG benefits such as improved health and well being, reduced time for fuel collection and cooking for women, and improved educational possibilities and outcomes. Specifically, health benefits arise from the reduction in hazards from indoor air pollution (smoke), and improved rights and educational outcomes are obtained from the reduction in time spent collecting fuelwood.

       The 'Mbaula za Makono, Banja la thanzi' project in Malawi aims to reduce wood consumption for cooking, thereby mitigating deforestation and improving health outcomes by providing cleaner, more efficient cooking solutions.

column2: GS12239 GS12240 RVPA-1 Amazi Meza Rwanda Water Supply Project For Schools
column9: GS Methodology for emission reductions from safe drinking water supply
column165: The objectives of this project are: (i) Schools from rural communities have access to safe water and (ii) CO2 Emissions are avoided. This project will address critical access to safe water, whilst contributing to pollution reduction through the benefits of carbon financing. The water purification systems will reduce both the use of and demand for firewood and other fuels used to boil drinking water, leading to reduction of carbon dioxide emissions. The project activities managed by Virridy will distribute, install and service low GHG emitting water purification systems at point-of-use (POU) to provide safe drinking water (SDW) for institutional application at schools in approximately five hundred (500) schools countrywide. The project technology will be installed at the POU within facilities of the schools (mostly, primary and secondary schools, other educational institutions can be included).

column2: Koalisation community based clean cooking program
column9: GS Simplified Methodology for Clean and Efficient Cookstoves
column165:
The Koalisation community based clean cooking program in Ndola aims to address the challenges associated with traditional charcoal usage in peri urban areas. The project focuses on promoting the adoption of improved cookstoves with a thermal efficiency of 71% as an alternative to traditional charcoal stoves. By introducing these clean cooking stoves, the project aims to achieve multiple benefits, including reducing the demand for charcoal, improving indoor air quality and so human health, and mitigating the negative environmental impacts associated with traditional cooking methods.
The project will involve the distribution of 2.900 improved cookstoves to households in peri urban areas of Ndola. To enhance the engagement with the community, an info point was built within the compound, to support the distribution of clean cooking stoves and to establish training programs to educate and raise awareness among community members about the benefits of using improved cookstoves. A solar water tower was built to provide safe drinkable water to the community. Furthermore a fruit trees nursery was built to host more than 5.000 plants that once ready, will be planted in the beneficiarie's backyards to improve food security and boost up biodiversity.

column2: GS11329 VPA-2 Beam Mobility- Micromobility VPA in Republic of Korea
column9: AMS-III.BM. Lightweight two and three wheeled personal transportation
column165: The VPA aims to implement an e-scooter sharing program and/or introduce e-bikes and e-mopeds within the geographical boundaries of host country under the master PoA GS11329.  This initiative seeks to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by replacing the use of private / public, fossil fuel-based vehicles with electric micromobility vehicles and promote sustainable mobility.

column2: AGROFORESTRY – CLIMATE PROOFING FARM LIVELIHOODS BY INFOSYS
column9: GS Methodology for Afforestation/Reforestation GHG Emissions Reduction and Sequestration
column165: The project is an agroforestry initiative across multiple states of India that aims to establish and increase vegetation cover by planting native tree species. column2: PoA Sustainable Landscapes and Forests Initiatives
column9: GS Methodology for Afforestation/Reforestation GHG Emissions Reduction and Sequestration
column15: ERDA ILLUMINE LOW CARBON SOLUTIONS PRIVATE LIMITED
column165:
This PoA aims to improve vegetation cover, arrest soil degradation, enhance soil quality and direct-indirect ecosystem services while creating income generation opportunities for communities through various livelihood activities. The program's objective is to restore 100,000 ha area of degraded land with mixed native tree plantation in India and Benin. The plantation model will be adopted based on local site specific biophysical and socioeconomical conditions and incorporates local ecological knowledge which is more important to implement the project. The specific developmental change that our above interventions will bring is sustained deceleration of climate change by restoring degraded land at large scale to shift to Land Degradation Neutrality and Net Zero Emission target.

Globally land degradation has affected more than 3.2 billion people living in rural areas with least possible adaptation options that has resulted in major biodiversity loss and ecosystem services. Without efforts to restore and protect land, nearly 70 gigatonnes more carbon would be emitted by 2050 due to land use change and soil degradation, representing approximately 17 per cent of current annual greenhouse gas emissions. 

In the baseline we have land lying fallow, degraded land due to continued deforestation and soil degradation because of extensive cattle grazing, land development works, poor farming and water harvesting practices, and so on. Also, small landowners/ farmers are not actively engaged in soil health restoration or afforestation/agroforestry projects which are crucial for effective climate-change mitigation. In the marginalised community sector who are heavily dependent on natural resources, awareness of plantation activity still being less at the national level and the upfront capital constraints pose as big barriers to the adoption and penetration of plantation activity. By linking these marginalised communities to carbon marketplaces, this PoA aims to overcome these critical barriers to adoption by enabling additional income opportunities to the community.

column165:
Hanbao Compost Project aims to prevent methane emissions associated with pig manure. The best use of pig manure is to mix it with other agricultural waste materials in appropriate proportions, composting it into high-quality fertilizer to be returned to the soil. This process not only facilitates resource recycling but also reduces the environmental pollution caused by pig manure. While it is a micro-scale project, it contributes to reducing global warming and generating carbon credits.

column2: COLAREZA - FMNR & Reforestation - VPA01
column165: World Vision Australia (WVA), World Vision Zambia (WVZ) and FORLIANCE intend to implement this Program of Activities with the objective to restore forest landscapes in several regions in Zambia making use of Assisted Natural Regeneration and other forest restoration and management methods. The POA seeks to create and enhance carbon sinks, reduce pressure on woody biomass, restore the local ecology and biodiversity and apply measures of climate smart agriculture whilst delivering significant socio-economic benefits to the local communities. The intent is to develop community-led revegetation projects using primarily Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) on degraded community land to ensure longterm social benefits and carbon removal. FMNR is a low cost, sustainable land restoration technique used to combat poverty and hunger among poor subsistence farmers by increasing food and timber production, and resilience to climate extremes. FMNR promotes the regrowth of indigenous trees, shrubs and naturally occurring seeds in degraded forest and farmland through farmers and community members undertaking selective pruning and protection to encourage the growth of new shoots. Since 2017 the FMNR technique has been promoted by WV'Z to be used by farmers in Miombo forest ecosystems of Zambia. The development of a carbon program is expected to accelerate the adoption of the technique and provide additional incentives for long term sustainability and permanence.

column2: Small Farmers' Carbon Farming in Noto's Satoyama Japan
column9: VMD0021 Estimation of Stocks in the Soil Carbon Pool
column165:
The Noto Peninsula is a symbolic landmark of the Satoyama Initiative, based on the concept of a traditional rural landscape where human activities and nature have coexisted sustainably for centuries in Japan. In 2024, the region was significantly impacted by natural disasters such as earthquakes, tsunamis, floods, and landslides, which compromised the sustainability of Noto's Satoyama.
In response to these events, the Tzu Chi Charity Foundation launched a relief program immediately after the January 1, 2024, Noto earthquakes to support local evacuated residents and communities. The foundation contributed 2.2 billion Japanese Yen to assist senior citizens in these communities. Recognizing the endangerment of Satoyama farming communities, Tzu Chi initiated a sustainable project modeled after the Gold Standard-listed Small Farmers' Carbon Farming Project in Taiwan (GS11818), utilizing the GS4GG's SDG Impact Tool to guide and measure the revitalization of Noto's Satoyama.
Gold Standard Soil Organic Carbon Framework Methodology is introduced to local farmers.  This project faces numerous challenges and requires innovative approaches. The preservation of the traditional Satoyama farming system and the introduction of carbon farming measures are equally crucial and mutually beneficial components of this initiative. The Satoyama Initiative has global significance, and all project participants invite anyone interested to be part of this endeavor.

column2: Installation of high efficiency wood burning cookstoves in Kenya
column9: Other
column15: Bridge Carbon Africa Stoves Development Private Limited
column165:
The project involves distribution of fuel-efficient improved cookstoves (ICS) in Republic of Kenya. The ICS disseminated through this project will replace the baseline practice of burning wood in rudimentary cookstoves or in three-stone fires.  Under this project, two Total Land Care (TLC) Rocket Stoves will be installed in eligible households throughout rural Kenya. The TLC Stove burns wood more efficiently than baseline stoves resulting in wood fuel savings for the user. 

The introduction of TLC Stoves saves both fuel costs and time spent on firewood collection. Time saved can be utilized for other productive activities such as exploring educational opportunities, attending school (for children), socializing, resting, or even home-based enterprises that generate additional income for households – all of which can lead to economic empowerment.  

The reduction of household air pollution, resulting from using the ICS, helps reduce the burden of disease (including respiratory, cardiovascular, and cognitive diseases) associated with exposure to household air pollution. Reduced morbidity results in fewer workdays lost for the country, reduced healthcare costs, and improved overall quality of life. 

As the ICS consume less firewood, it will help prevent excessive firewood consumption and reduce forest degradation. This reduction in demand for wood fuel allows forests to regenerate, protecting wildlife habitats and biodiversity.

column2: Renqiu Geothermal Central Heating System
column165:
The project activity is designed to introduce geothermal energy based space heating system to realize heat supply to a series of new residential buildings in Renqiu County over winter season, which will displace heat supply from isolated coal-fired boilers as a business-as-usual scenario in the project area.

Renqiu County is in Cangzhou City of Hebei Province. The proposed project will involve the construction and operation of geothermal production wells, reinjection wells, heat substations and heat supply pipelines. 

The project owner is PetroChina Co., Ltd. Xiong'an Branch and it will put into operation in November 2025 (winter season). column2: Reduction of Methane Emissions through Manure Composting at KOFERT ORGANIC Baicoi - Romania
column9: AMS-III.F. Avoidance of methane emissions through composting
column165:
KOFERT ORGANIC SRL is developing an innovative project in Baicoi, Prahova County, to produce solid organic fertilizer using 100% natural materials. The project aims to expand the capacity of the existing composting plant, recovering organic waste through aerobic fermentation, contributing to sustainable agriculture and environmental protection.

By utilizing Japanese Kohshin KNLL-6000 SHW technology, the plant ensures efficient and accelerated composting of animal manure, transforming it into a stable, granular, and hygienic fertilizer. The high-temperature process eliminates pathogens and prevents seed germination in the compost.

The resulting organic fertilizer is rich in essential nutrients and organic matter, with a balanced pH that enhances soil structure and water retention. Its use helps reduce atmospheric carbon and supports sustainable farming practices.

Through this project, KOFERT ORGANIC SRL provides a sustainable solution for managing organic waste and improving soil quality, strengthening partnerships with livestock farms and agricultural enterprises.

column2: Reduction of Methane Emissions through Manure Composting at KOFERT ORGANIC Mihailesti - Romania
column165:
KOFERT ORGANIC SRL is developing an organic fertilizer production project in Mihăilești, Giurgiu County, using advanced Japanese Kohshin composting lines type KNLL-6000 SHW technology. The process involves aerobic fermentation of poultry manure and organic waste, ensuring a stable, hygienic, and nutrient-rich fertilizer.

The project will be implemented in phases, starting with the installation of a composting line, followed by an expansion to increase processing capacity. The facility will also include sorting and packaging lines for various product formats. The technology ensures efficient manure processing, eliminating pathogens and preventing seed germination while maintaining high-quality organic content.

The final product is a balanced organic fertilizer enriched with essential nutrients, improving soil structure, enhancing water retention, and supporting sustainable agriculture. By promoting carbon sequestration and increasing soil fertility, this initiative contributes to environmental sustainability while offering an effective solution for managing livestock waste and improving agricultural productivity.

column2: GS11638 GS11640 RVPA-10 SPOUTS Water Purifier Programme in Africa-WPS in Uganda by AERA-VPA 20

column2: ReNew Sakhi 04-Electric Cooking Project-01
column9: GS Methodology for Metered and Measured Energy Cooking Devices
column165:
Household air pollution is a global crisis and India is not unaffected by the problem. There is significant dependence on polluting traditional cookstoves for cooking in rural and semi-urban households in the country. Household pollution can cause diseases and women are particularly affected due to their direct exposure to cooking fires and involvement in daily cooking. Combustion of non-renewable fuels and the release of greenhouse gas emissions into the environment adds to the global warming problem. 

The proposed project activity will address this problem by distributing induction stoves to the target households in Kerela, India. The purpose of the project activity is to decrease fuel wood consumption by replacing inefficient traditional cookstoves and LPG stoves in 1,00,000 households with efficient induction stoves starting with pilot of 1000 Induction cookstove deployment.

column2: Navoi 1-2 Solar Power Plant
column15: GAİA CLİMATE FİNANSAL DANIŞMANLIK HİZMETLERİ VE TİCARET ANONİM ŞİRKETİ
column165: The NAVOI-1-2 Solar Power Plant Project is a large-scale renewable energy initiative designed to support Uzbekistan's transition toward clean energy and contribute to the global effort to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The purpose of the project is to generate electricity by using clean solar power resources to meet the national electricity demand. The expected annual GHG emission reductions over the first crediting period are 554,070 tCO2e/yr, that will contribute to the alleviation of climate change effects. NAVOI-1-2 Solar Power Plant will contribute to the achievement of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy), SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) and SDG 13 (Climate Action).

column2: Earthbond Nigeria Distributed Solar for Productive Use
column165:
Lagos has around 4.7 million gensets, which emit an estimated 39 million tonnes of CO2 per year. The reliance on gensets for electricity due to insufficient grid availability leads to health issues and costs Nigerians ₦7.6 trillion on fuel and maintenance. The average small to medium business spends ~₦50,000-400,000 per month just on fuel.

This is not just an energy crisis. It is a missed opportunity for economic growth, environmental sustainability, and global leadership.

Earthbond, a climate tech start-up based in Lagos, is implementing a distributed solar project in Nigeria to reduce reliance on expensive and polluting gensets. Earthbond provides a digital one-stop-shop which removes the complexity and cost for over 45 million African businesses who need to switch to clean, affordable, and reliable energy.
As well as the economic and health benefits, solar installations and the displacement of gensets will lead to a reduction in CO2 emissions. 

The technology includes solar PV systems which are suitable for micro, small and medium sized enterprises (MSMEs). The project aims to reach thousands of businesses across Nigeria and will last for 15 years.

The Earthbond Distributed Solar project will create significant economic, social and environmental impact by reducing the costs associated with electricity supply, remove exposure to smoke and carbon monoxide, and reduce CO2 emissions.

column2: Niger Delta Community-Driven Mangrove Restoration Project
column165:
The Niger Delta Community-Driven Mangrove Restoration Project is a scalable initiative focused on restoring the historically mangrove-rich wetlands of the Niger Delta through a community-led approach.

The Niger Delta—the largest river delta in Africa and home to the world's third-largest mangrove forest—has faced severe degradation over the past decades due to a variety of pressures. This has compromised biodiversity, diminished livelihoods, and increased vulnerability to flooding and erosion for the 30 million people who live there.

This Programme of Activities aims to restore the ecosystem through training local communities to plant native, locally adapted mangrove species, while also addressing the causes of mangrove loss.

Its objectives are to: 
• Empower communities by providing the livelihood support, education, and tools needed to become long-term ecosystem stewards and bolster their resilience in a climate-changing world, 
• Restore a critical ecosystem and its services while promoting biodiversity by rebuilding the habitats of numerous species, strengthening regional food security, and providing flood and storm protection. 
• And finally, sequester carbon in the fight against climate change while utilizing mangroves as a powerful nature-based solution.

Rooted in strong local partnerships and ecosystem restoration approaches, the project is designed to scale and serve as a model for community-first restoration across Nigeria and the wider region.

column2: Duguna Fango and Damot Weyde Assisted Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration for Sustainable Land Management and Livelihood Improvement Project
column9: GS Methodology for Afforestation/Reforestation GHG Emissions Reduction and Sequestration
column165: The "Duguna Fango and Damot Weyde Assisted Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration for Sustainable Land Management and Livelihood Improvement Project" aims to regenerate and reforest degraded land in the Duguna Fango and Damot Weyde Woredas of South Ethiopia Regional State of Ethiopia. The area has undergone extensive environmental degradation in the past few decades due to overgrazing, farmland and settlement expansion, timber logging, firewood collection, charcoal production, and forest fire. The project will apply the assisted 'Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR)' technique to reforest degraded lands in the target areas. FMNR is a low-cost, sustainable, and simple practice that communities can use to restore their land, increase its productivity, and build resilience within the community. FMNR is the systematic re-growth and management of trees from felled stumps, sprouting root systems or seeds remaining in the soils from cleared forests, or in woody thickets. FMNR is an empowering form of social forestry which gives individuals and communities both responsibility for care and nurture of naturally occurring woody vegetation and rewards from sustainable harvesting of wood and NTFP. A FMNR project ideally involves the entire community or landscape and is a practice that contributes to a range of desired development outcomes such as land restoration, sustainable agricultural production systems, livelihood and community development and climate mitigation and adaptation.

column2: Brújula Verde
column165:
Brújula Verde is a large-scale, 30,000-hectare reforestation and ecosystem restoration project in Vichada, Colombia, designed to deliver high-integrity nature-based carbon removals while supporting biodiversity and community development. The project focuses on establishing diverse, mixed-species forests through the planting of both fast-growing pioneer species and a wide range of native trees, 
ultimately transitioning toward predominantly native forest cover. This approach enhances soil recovery, 
improves water and nutrient cycles, and builds long-term landscape resilience. By combining phased 
planting and enrichment strategies, Brújula Verde strengthens ecosystem services, contributes to 
Colombia's climate mitigation goals, and generates local employment and sustainable livelihood 
opportunities

column165: The Programme of Activity includes the sale, distribution and utilization of high-efficiency biomass burning technologies such as improved cookstoves and dryers in Vietnam. column165: The Project includes the sale, distribution and utilization of high-efficiency dryers in Thai Nguyen, Viet Nam to promote the sustainable green tea processing. column2: Ghana Household Carbon Reduction Programme (GHCRP)
column165: The purpose of the proposed mitigation activity is to provide residential users (HH) with energy-efficient cooking technology i.e., tier 5 Improved Charcoal Stoves (ICS) and safe water drinking systems that reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from the combustion of non-renewable woody biomass-based charcoal for cooking or boiling of water in Ghana. It also seeks to address water contamination issues, that heavily impact households, by providing a safe water source. Depending on the criticality of needs within the household, they will either be targeted with ICS or safe water drinking systems. The project will also provide financial savings for the HH, because of a reduction in charcoal consumption and will improve their health by reducing the exposure to indoor air pollution (IAP).

column2: GS PoA Safe Water Programme in East Africa-Uganda
column165:

The "Agroforestry Carbon Program for Resilient Himalayan Communities" aims to
restore approximately 6,430 hectares of long-abandoned agricultural land in Nepal's
mid-hill and Terai regions through the introduction of agroforestry species and the
promotion of sustainable practices like intercropping. The project will be carried out
in areas where much of the land has remained uncultivated for years and is owned
by small to medium-scale farmers. The key objectives of the project includes:
• Promotion of sustainable agroforestry practices that contribute to restoration of
agricultural land and improved productivity.
• The introduction of high-value tree species and linking farmers to market-oriented
agroforestry products, with an aim to improve their livelihoods and create long-term

column2: Tasar tree-based Afforestation for livelihood Sustainability And carbon Removal (TASAR)
column165:
The TASAR Project is an afforestation initiative designed to restore degraded and barren lands through the establishment of diverse forest tree plantations on privately owned lands belonging to marginalized communities as recognized in the Indian Constitution. Over a five-year period (2023–2027), the project aims to cover 15,200 hectares of fallow or degraded land, positively impacting approximately 14,000 farmers across 600 villages.
This initiative promotes the planting of indigenous host tree species for the Tasar silkworm (Antheraea mylitta Drury). The tree species planted will enhance biodiversity by improving habitat quality, stabilizing soil, and supporting pollinators and wildlife. Their diverse canopy and flowering cycles further support ecosystem resilience. Terminalia arjuna and Terminalia tomentosa serve as primary host species for the Tasar silkworm. These native trees, known for their longevity exceeding 50 years, thrive in depleted soils and effectively support Tasar silkworm rearing. Their robust growth also contributes to large-scale atmospheric CO₂ sequestration, enhancing climate change mitigation efforts. The initiative is expected to create a sustainable source of income for the participating farmers as the host trees support Tasar silkworm rearing, offering farmers a reliable source of income through the sale of silk cocoons, moth eggs known as seeds, and Tasar silk.

column2: Recovery of metals and minerals from incinerator bottom ash in Switzerland
column165: The project includes the construction and operation of metal and mineral recovery plants in Switzerland. Each plant has the capacity to process thousands of tons of incinerator bottom ash (IBA) from nearby incinerators on an annual basis. Around half of materials from the incinerator waste are set to be recovered, among which is a significant share of valuable metals and mineral fractions. The recovered metal and mineral fractions are sold downstream and therefore re-enter the economic cycle. The activity results in the reduction of emissions through the replacement of virgin materials in manufacturing, avoiding emissions involved in the extraction and processing of such materials.

column2: SuWASH Ghana: Enhancing Sustainable Access to Safe Drinking Water
column165:
Multiple water supply systems, originally designed to serve a combined population of approximately 45,000 people across 12 villages in Ghana's Eastern and Ashanti regions, have fallen into a state of disrepair due to prolonged lack of maintenance and weak operational management. As a result, the systems are now considered practically inoperable, with significantly reduced functionality.
The infrastructure includes boreholes with submersible pumps, elevated water storage tanks, interconnected distribution pipelines and communal tap stations. These systems were initially developed through a private sector initiative and later transferred to the Ghana Red Cross Society. However, the receiving entity faced ongoing challenges related to limited technical capacity and financial constraints, which hindered the systems' maintenance and long-term performance.

column2: UHI "YUEDIAN 83"  Shipping Retrofit Project
column15: Beijing MD Energy Technology Co. Ltd.
column165:
The Project comprises the application of one or more energy efficiency measures 
as retrofits to existing ships. The types of eligible retrofit measures include Design related measures、Propulsion measures、Machinery measures、Operating measures etc. These measures would reduce fossil fuel consumption and thereby reduce CO2 emissions. 
Since the ship in this project travels in international waters, shipping emissions and emissions reduction are not included in the GHG inventory of any country usually. The International Maritime Organisation (IMO, belonging to the UN) is responsible for setting commitments on emissions from ships, there is no Host Country for these 
projects. 
Moreover, there is no physical geographical location of the project activity. However, the ship has a unique identification number established by the IMO. As stated in Section "Baseline Methodology: Project Boundary" of the methodology "Retrofit Energy Efficiency Measures in Shipping": "The spatial project boundary is the geographical location of project ships in which vessels are clearly identified by their unique IMO-Number." 
.The proposed project is considered to be micro scale, since the expected emissions reductions are below 10,000 tCO2eq/year.

column2: Nature-based Solutions for Regenerated Forests and Community Resilience in Ethiopia
column165:
World Vision Australia intends to implement this Programme of Activities (PoA) for afforestation and reforestation activities in several states of Ethiopia. 

The PoA aims to regenerate degraded land through the implementation of the Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) practice and enrichment planting (described in the section A.3). By sequestering carbon, the PoA contributes to climate change mitigation efforts while improving local biodiversity, soil fertility, and water retention. These interventions aim to provide long-term benefits to local communities by creating sustainable livelihoods and promoting ecosystem services.

column2: Nature-based Solutions for Regenerated Forests and Community Resilience in Ethiopia - Chifra 01
column165:

This project will be developed as a Voluntary Project Activity (VPA) under the Gold Standard Programme of Activities (PoA): "Nature-based Solutions for Regenerated Forests and Community Resilience in Ethiopia". 

The project aims to restore the degraded rangelands in the Chifra Woreda by utilising Farmer-Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) as a primary approach, with the inclusion of enrichment planting, involving cultivating seedlings in nurseries.

column2: Azimayi Improved Cookstoves in the Republic of Malawi
column165:
Azimayi Improved Cookstoves in the Republic of Malawi" is a large-scale project that aims to distribute energy-efficient improved cooking solutions (ICS) in domestic households and communities in the Republic of Malawi (project location), thereby replacing traditional inefficient cooking devices that utilize firewood as a primary cooking fuel in the baseline. 

Traditional cooking methods (use of inefficient, solid biomass cooking devices like 3-stone fires/ open fires and/or traditional solid fuel stoves) prevalent across the Republic of Malawi generate significant volumes of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions attributed to the inefficient combustion of unsustainably sourced, non-renewable biomass (NRB) fuel.

The project activity includes the dissemination of project ICS to beneficiaries using traditional modes of cooking in the baseline. The project ICS employs natural draft technology to improve fuel combustion, aiding better heat transfer to the cooking pots.

column2: Chestnut Sustainable Restoration Megaton Project
column165:
The United States is home to over 700 million acres of forestland, nearly 7.5% of the world's forests, that provide clean water, recreation, and other life-sustaining resources to Americans. The importance of American forests to the global ecosystem and climate is central to the work of CC Project SPV, LLC ("Project Developer"), a US-based company that seeks to restore and conserve functional forestland throughout the United States for the primary purpose of increasing carbon sequestration. 

Using the Gold Standard Land Use and Forest Activities Requirements and A/R (afforestation and reforestation) methodologies, the Project Developer is implementing an afforestation project called the Chestnut Sustainable Restoration Megaton Project on multiple parcels of land within the United States. The Project Developer will be acquiring and leasing unproductive, intensively managed pasture and croplands to plant trees and restore diverse, native forests. The purpose of the project is to increase carbon stocks and sequester greenhouse gases while creating sustainably managed native forestland throughout the country. The Project Developer has extensive expertise in carbon project development and forest management. The Project Developer's employees will manage planted forests and maintain the project's Forest Stewardship Council certification.

column2: GS12494 GS12495 RVPA 1 Improved Cookstove Distribution in Rajasthan and Gujarat by Alphabet Greens
column165: The VPA aims to provide end-users with affordable and highly adaptable clean cooking solutions. This initiative targets reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from the burning of non-renewable woody biomass for household cooking and heating. Additionally, the project envisions benefiting household members, particularly women, by lowering exposure to indoor air pollution, reducing healthcare expenses, and alleviating the drudgery of firewood collection, purchase, and use. Developed under the Gold Standard, this project ensures high social impact on the community, leading to large-scale local socio-economic benefits while achieving verifiable emission reductions.

column2: RANOVOLA Water Program
column165:
The RANOVOLA project, building on infrastructure put in place by other HELVETAS initiatives, aims to ensure safe and sustainable access to clean water for the most vulnerable rural communities in Madagascar. 
The RANOVOLA project main objectives are to provide reliable access to clean water, improve public health by reducing the prevalence of waterborne diseases, strengthen the autonomy of local communities by collaborating with private operators to manage the operation and maintenance of the established infrastructure, support the ecological transition by limiting dependence on fossil fuels and firewood for water purification, and contribute to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by acting on health, environmental, economic, and social fronts. 
The RANOVOLA project infrastructure will rely on two main technologies: 1) gravitational systems, using water sources located at higher altitudes to transport water to communities without the need for additional energy; and 2) solar pumping systems, utilizing boreholes to ensure a constant and economical water supply. 
In both cases, water treatment is carried out by filtration, chlorination, and iron removal. The operation and management of the infrastructure will be ensured by private operators, under a decentralized management model in compliance with Malagasy legal frameworks.

column2: Sarkylmas Kuat Wind Power Project
column165: The Sarkylmas Kuat Wind Power Project is a greenfield Independent Power Project located in the Mangystau Region of Kazakhstan. The Project involves the construction and operation of a 50 MW wind farm to provide renewable energy to Kazakhstan's national electricity grid(KEGOC).

column2: Enabling Clean Energy Transitions Through BESS Integration
column165: The project involves the deployment of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) to store electricity generated from renewable energy sources such as solar or wind. The BESS enables time-shifting of renewable energy by storing surplus electricity during periods of low demand and discharging it during peak demand periods or grid stress events. This reduces the need for fossil fuel-based peaking power plants and supports grid stability and renewable energy integration. The system comprises battery, power conversion systems (inverters), battery management systems, and control software to optimize charging/discharging cycles. The project contributes to greenhouse gas (GHG) emission reductions by displacing grid electricity that would otherwise be generated from fossil fuels.

column2: Promoting Regenerative Agriculture for Nature (PRAN)
column165: Promoting Regenerative Agriculture for Nature (PRAN)" is a Programme of Activities (PoA) to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from rice farming based on traditional practices like continuous flooding in India. The PoA will implement improved water management techniques, such as intermittent flooding, alternate wetting and drying (AWD), direct seeded rice (DSR) and regenerative farming practices etc. in rice paddies across India.  The PoA applies the Gold Standard Methodology for methane emission Reduction by adjusted water management practice in rice cultivation, version 1.0.

column2: VPA 01 Low carbon rice farming in India
column165: The proposed Voluntary Project Activity (VPA) is developed by Grow Indigo Private Limited and is implemented across states of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh in India. VPA implements improved water management techniques, such as intermittent flooding, alternate wetting and drying (AWD), direct seeded rice (DSR) and regenerative farming practices, etc. in rice paddies. This initiative aims to introduce and promote improved agricultural techniques specifically for rice farming, falling under the Land Use & Forestry (LUF) and Agriculture (AGR) categories.

column2: Restore Africa: Restoring Landscapes and Livelihoods in Western Uganda
column165:
The Restore Africa: Restoring Landscapes and Livelihoods in Western Uganda project is implemented in degraded agricultural landscapes in the Western (Afromontane) highlands and pastoral rangelands of mid-Western Uganda. Over several decades, these regions have experienced substantial deforestation and degradation, poor agriculture practices, overgrazing, and an unsustainable demand for fuelwood. Climate change, population increases, poverty and lack of economic opportunities further exacerbate pressure on the land. 
The project focuses on establishment of new trees (e.g. through manual planting and broadcast seeding) as well as the improved management activities that enhance the natural regeneration of established root stock (e.g. through coppice management) in 24 districts in Western Uganda involving more than 200,000 small farmer households. The aim is to both sequester carbon as well as generate a broad set of environmental and socio-economic co-benefits through the implementation of sustainable agroforestry practices at a landscape scale. Co-benefits, based on the restoration of ecosystem functions, include sustainable food production, enhanced local livelihoods, increased gender equality and the improvement of ecosystem services.
The project will collaborate and align with the many organizations already established in the area to enhance long-term sustainability and ensure that implementation occurs in an efficient, locally appropriate, and acceptable manner.

column2: Restore Africa: Restoring Landscapes and Livelihoods in Malawi
column165:
The Restore Africa: Restoring Landscapes and Livelihoods in Malawi project is implemented in degraded agricultural landscapes in the in the Northern, Central and Southern Regions of the country. Over 90% of households in the country depend on natural resources and subsistence agriculture to meet their livelihoods, food and energy needs. Extensive clearing of forest and woodlands for fuelwood, followed by conversion to cropland, is driving a high annual deforestation rate of 1%.
The project focuses on establishment of new trees (e.g. through manual planting and broadcast seeding) as well as the improved management activities that enhance the natural regeneration of established root stock (e.g. through coppice management) in seven districts in Malawi involving more than 150,000 small farmer households. The aim is to both sequester carbon as well as generate a broad set of environmental and socio-economic co-benefits through the implementation of sustainable agroforestry practices at a landscape scale. Co-benefits, based on the restoration of ecosystem functions, include sustainable food production, enhanced local livelihoods, increased gender equality and the improvement of ecosystem services.
The project will collaborate and align with the many organizations already established in the area to enhance long-term sustainability and ensure that implementation occurs in an efficient, locally appropriate, and acceptable manner.

column2: Restore Africa: Restoring Landscapes and Livelihoods in Coastal Kenya
column165:
The Restore Africa: Restoring Landscapes and Livelihoods in Coastal Kenya project is implemented in Kenya's coastal region, specifically in the Kwale and Kilifi counties. With an annual deforestation rate of 0.58%, Kenya faces significant forest loss, primarily driven by dependence on natural resources and extensive land degradation.  The primary causes of land degradation include unsustainable wood resource exploitation, the expansion of unsustainable cultivation practices, the spread of invasive species, pollution, and climate change.
The project focuses on establishment of new trees (e.g. through manual planting and broadcast seeding) as well as the improved management activities that enhance the natural regeneration of established root stock (e.g. through coppice management) in the Kwale and Kilifi counties in Kenya, involving more than 100,000 small farmer households. The aim is to both sequester carbon as well as generate a broad set of environmental and socio-economic co-benefits through the implementation of sustainable agroforestry practices at a landscape scale. Co-benefits, based on the restoration of ecosystem functions, include increased household income, enhanced local livelihoods, increased gender equality and the improvement of ecosystem services.
The project builds on extensive experience in socio-economic development within the region.

column2: Landfill gas recovery energy generation and  biogas distribution from CTR Santa Rosa
column15: CICLUS AMBIENTAL DO BRASIL S A
column165:
1. Project Design and Scenarios
The project aims to collect and treat landfill gas (Landfill Gas – LFG) in various scenarios to reduce methane emissions. The planned scenarios include:
•Controlled flaring of collected gas;
•Supplying treated gas to industrial, commercial, or residential consumers;
•Using gas as fuel for electricity generation.
These scenarios will be applied according to the specific characteristics and needs of each landfill included in the program.
At the Santa Rosa Waste Treatment Center (CTR) in Seropédica (Rio de Janeiro – Brazil), the current scenario involves the capture of landfill gas (LFG) for combustion and distribution to external consumers. In the future, infrastructure is planned for electricity generation from the collected gas.
2. Technologies and Measures
The project uses modern technologies for LFG capture, treatment, and utilization, such as:
•Vertical and horizontal wells for gas collection;
•High-efficiency flaring systems;
•Infrastructure for gas treatment, including contaminant removal;
•Infrastructure for transporting biogas by trucks for external thermal applications.
For future phases, CTR Santa Rosa also plans to install modular equipment for electricity generation.
Additionally, the project includes strict monitoring to ensure operational efficiency and safety.
3. Geographic Boundaries
Currently, the project only includes CTR Santa Rosa in Seropédica/RJ. Geographic coordinates: -22.795703 (latitude) and -43.760558 (longitude).

By reducing the amount of firewood required for cooking, the project alleviates the time and physical burden of firewood collection—a task that disproportionately falls on women and girls. In addition to reducing greenhouse gas emissions, the project delivers a range of co-benefits, including: Improved indoor air quality, reducing the incidence of respiratory and eye-related illnesses caused by smoke inhalation from traditional stoves. Reduced pressure on local forests through decreased firewood demand, slowing deforestation and preserving biodiversity. Lower household expenditure on cooking fuel due to more efficient wood use. Increased time savings for women and children, enabling greater focus on education, caregiving, and economic activities. Job creation and skill development through local cookstove production and distribution. By addressing both climate change and local development needs, the project contributes to eight Sustainable Development Goals.

column2: Niger Delta Community-Driven Mangrove Restoration [Real Case VPA]
column165: The Niger Delta Community-Driven Mangrove Restoration Project is a scalable initiative focused on restoring the historically mangrove-rich wetlands of the Niger Delta through a community-led approach. The Niger Delta—the largest river delta in Africa and home to the world's third-largest mangrove forest—has faced severe degradation over the past decades due to a variety of pressures. This has compromised biodiversity, diminished livelihoods, and increased vulnerability to flooding and erosion for the 30 million people who live there. This project aims to restore the ecosystem through training local communities to plant native, locally adapted mangrove species, while also addressing the causes of mangrove loss. Its objectives are to: • Empower communities by providing the livelihood support, education, and tools needed to become long-term ecosystem stewards and bolster their resilience in a climate-changing world, • Restore a critical ecosystem and its services while promoting biodiversity by rebuilding the habitats of numerous species, strengthening regional food security, and providing flood and storm protection. • And finally, sequester carbon in the fight against climate change while utilizing mangroves as a powerful nature-based solution. Rooted in strong local partnerships and ecosystem restoration approaches, the project is designed to scale and serve as a model for community-first restoration across Nigeria and the wider region.

column2: Project Saladillo: Sustainable Mosaic Afforestation Operation in Eastern Paraguay
column165:
Project Saladillo transforms 15,946 hectares of cattle grazing land, subject to continual slash-and-burn practices, in Paraguay's Cordillera region into a mosaic plantation combining commercial and conservation forestry. It prioritises long-term ecological resilience and sustainable development. The project integrates 25% permanent conservation with 75% selectively harvested forestry, maintaining at least 96% continuous forest cover. This model prevents deforestation by producing sustainable timber and biomass, while enhancing biodiversity through protection of native forests and riparian corridors, supporting habitat continuity and safeguarding local fauna.
An estimated 1,122,437 tons of CO₂ will be sequestered over 50+ years. High-precision carbon monitoring uses LiDAR-based models calibrated with field sampling to ensure accuracy in both accessible and remote areas.
Saladillo generates formal, year-round employment through staggered planting and harvesting, eliminating informal labour, reducing seasonal risks, and ensuring steady income for local communities. It collaborates closely with local NGOs such as Fundación Moisés Bertoni and the University of Asunción, integrating community engagement, biodiversity monitoring, and academic research.
The project adheres to the highest environmental and social safeguards, aligning with FSC certification, IFC Performance Standards, and World Bank guidelines, contributing to SDGs 8, 12, 13, and 15.

column165: In most of the countries on the African continent including Ghana, cooking is done on either 3-stone fires or very inefficient traditional cookstoves, consuming a lot of fuel, in particular non-renewable firewood and charcoal. The high biomass consumption has negative impacts on the environment leading to deforestation and land degradation, Greenhouse Gas Emissions (GHG) emissions, loss of soil fertility and soils' reduced ability of water retention. Further, indoor air pollution through health-damaging pollutants while combusting firewood and charcoal result in diseases like e.g. pneumonia, stroke, ischemic heart diseases, chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases and lung cancer. The purpose of a 'STERLING IMPROVED COOKSTOVES PROJECT Carbon Project Activities included under the Gold Standard', is to disseminate highly efficient improved cookstoves (ICS to urban, peri-urban and/or rural users (households, communities, institutions, or SMEs) in Ghana. Several greenhouse gases (GHG), including carbon dioxide, are produced as a result of the incomplete combustion of biomass as used in cook stoves. More GHG emissions result from the use of biomass which is non-renewable. ICS improves heat transfer efficiency as compared to the baseline traditional cook stoves, thereby reducing both the amount of woody biomass used by unit appliances implemented and the emission of GHGs.

column2: Ghana Cocoa Agroforestry Livelihoods Project
column165:
The Ghana Cocoa Agroforestry Livelihoods Project is designed to enhance the productivity and long-term sustainability of cocoa farming systems while improving the livelihoods of the communities that depend on them. By introducing an agroforestry model that integrates shade tree species into existing cocoa plantations, the project aims to extend the productive lifespan of cocoa trees and strengthen the system's resilience to environmental challenges, including pests and diseases. This initiative will be carried out in close partnership with the local communities, with a focus on engaging youth teams to lead on the ground implementation. 
The project is expected to reach 11,000 farmers for an implementation area of 17,000 hectares. The project's main activity consists of planting shade and fruit trees within the existing cocoa plantations. Nine different native tree species will be incorporated into the farms to achieve a target density of 90 shade trees per hectare. 
Additionally, the new tree plantations will be associated with the training and coaching of the farmers in sustainable agroforestry practices such as tree management, pruning and Integrated Pest Management (IPM). The implementation of these practices is expected to increase the productive lifetime of the cocoa species and reduce the incidence of pests and diseases on the targeted trees. The project is expected to sequester 2.61 MtCO2e within 30 years.

column2: Accelerating Access to Clean Cooking in Kenya by Nyalore Impact Limited
column165:

The project intends to accelerate access to clean cooking by displacing use of inefficient biomass cooking devices and polluting fuels. Use of the project technology will displace GHG emissions from the thermal energy consumption required for cooking by households. This will consequently contribute towards reduced household air pollution and support several sustainable development goals. The project's primary target is end-users who cook using inefficient biomass cookstoves and polluting fuels such as kerosene both in the urban and rural areas of Kenya.

Goals and Objectives of the Project Activity
According to the 2022 KNBS Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) report, 68.5% of Kenyan population still highly dependent on traditional cooking fuels, with firewood being the predominant cooking fuel. This presents a climate change challenge and has motivated the project developer to develop an innovative project that will accelerate the transition to cleaner cooking solutions to mitigate the negative impacts associated with the use of traditional fuels.

column2: Agroforestry for Livelihoods and Climate Resilience in Odisha: A Joint Initiative by Infosys and SGI Foundation

Implemented by the SGI Foundation, the project aims to sequester atmospheric carbon dioxide through large-scale plantation activities, while simultaneously enhancing local biodiversity, improving soil health, and promoting sustainable livelihoods. Beyond its environmental benefits, the project contributes significantly to socio-economic development by generating temporary employment for community members during the plantation's establishment and maintenance phases. It also strengthens long-term sustainability through capacity-building and inclusive community engagement. The initiative supports multiple SDGs, including Climate Action (SDG 13), Life on Land (SDG 15), and No Poverty (SDG 1), by integrating carbon sequestration with biodiversity conservation and rural development. column2: Producción sostenible de biofertilizantes y biogás a partir de desechos de materia orgánica. Gran Canaria
column165:
The plant, located in the municipality of Agüimes, in Gran Canaria, is expected to come into operation in October 2025, at which time a three-month operational test phase will be carried out to guarantee the efficiency and safety of the process. The implementation to obtain emission reductions is estimated in the first quarter of 2026.
This first plant will be located next to the Southeast treatment plant, in the port free zone of Gran Canaria, which will facilitate its logistical integration and connectivity with distribution channels. It will be designed to manage up to 31,000 tonnes of organic waste per year, from which approximately 2,242 tonnes of biomethane per year will be produced, equivalent to 31,141 MWh of energy. This production of this energy vector represents a sustainable alternative to about 2,832 tons of propane gas, which will allow a significant reduction in the use of fossil fuels and polluting gas emissions and contribute to local climate and energy governance. 
As for the size and scope of the activity of the facility, it is estimated that it can serve some 45-65 hotels since the capacity of the digester, is 31,000 t/y of organic waste.
Among the key components of the project, the production of biomethane as a renewable substitute for propane gas and diesel stands out.

column15: University of Guam Center for Island Sustainability & Sea Grant (UOG CIS & SG)
column165:

column2: METHANE EMISSION REDUCTION BY AWD IN RICE FARMING IN CAMBODIA
column165:
This PoA aims to save water and reduce methane emissions during rice farming by introducing water management technology to rice farming, which is one of the main greenhouse gas emission sources in Cambodia.  By participating in this project, farmers can produce low-carbon rice without reducing rice productivity and participate in mitigating climate change.  ThanksCarbon, a business developer, has introduced an AI-based satellite technology into this project to reduce the burden on individual farmers for data collection and improve the convenience of monitoring data collection and MRV transparency.

Farmers will be motivated and trained to refrain from continuously flooding their fields by putting the suggested AWD technology into effect, which would cut down on the quantity of CH4 emissions that would have been produced in the baseline situation. The sole change made to the project scenario is the adoption of alternating wetting and drying conditions rather than the submerged condition. Other than that, the project keeps the current agricultural techniques in place and does not introduce any new activities that might increase greenhouse gas emissions.

column2: Avoiding methane emissions through composting at DN Agrar Romania
column165:
The "Avoiding Methane Emissions through Composting at DN Agrar, Romania" project aims to significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions by implementing controlled aerobic composting of raw dairy manure at two farms located in Alba and Hunedoara counties. Traditionally, manure is managed through open stockpiling or storage in lagoons, practices that lead to uncontrolled anaerobic decomposition and the release of methane (CH₄), a greenhouse gas with a global warming potential significantly higher than CO₂.

By diverting manure from these conventional methods and instead processing it through a structured composting system, the project prevents methane emissions at source. The composting process stabilizes the organic material, producing high-quality compost that can be applied to agricultural land. This not only improves soil health and fertility but also enhances the soil's carbon sequestration capacity, supporting long-term climate resilience in Romanian agriculture.

In summary, the project delivers both immediate climate benefits through methane avoidance and broader environmental co-benefits by promoting sustainable manure management and improving local soil systems.

The "GS PoA for Sustainable Rice Cultivation Projects in India" consists of implementation of Alternate and Wetting and Drying (AWD) practice in India. Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) method and aerobic rice cultivation method is a scientifically proven way of managing rice fields for better water management and achieving reduction or avoidance of methane emissions that is caused in traditional submerged rice fields. Therefore, Landmark Agri Exports Pvt. Ltd. (an Indian entity) & WeAct Pty Ltd. (an Australian entity) has taken a voluntary initiative to develop a project in India that is designed specifically for Rice fields to adopt AWD and other adjusted water managements methods, to be implemented across various states of India. Thus, the main objective of the project is to avoid flooded irrigation in rice fields and adopt AWD/other adjusted water management methods for rice cultivation to reduce methane emissions from the rice fields.

column2: VPA1-GS PoA for Sustainable Rice Cultivation Projects in India
column165:
The proposed project activity is the voluntary action undertaken by Landmark Agri Exports Pvt. Ltd., and WeAct Pty Ltd. The project falls under the Agriculture category introducing improved agricultural practices in rice cultivation.

This project aims to reduce methane (CH4) emissions through improved water management practices involving alternate wetting and drying (AWD) of the paddy lands. AWD is a proven method to reduce CH4 emission by as much as 48% compared to continuously flooded conditions where high rates of CH4 are emitted by the lands due to the anaerobic decomposition of the organic matter . Rice is the most prominent food crop in India. It is the backbone of livelihood for millions of rural households and plays a vital role in the country's food security. India is one of the world's largest producers and exporters of rice and hence plays an important part in the country's economy. The proposed VPA activity is planned to be implemented in the Madhya Pradesh State of India.

This VPA is implemented in Seoni district covering 26,103 ha in 8 tahsils

column2: Green Briquettes for Fossil Fuel Displacement in South Africa
column165: The proposed Programme of Activities (PoA) involves the production of biomass briquettes, with the objective of replacing conventional fossil fuels such as coal, furnace oil, and firewood commonly used by industries and institutions for thermal energy applications. The primary goal is to promote the use of clean, renewable, and sustainable biomass energy while reducing reliance on carbon-intensive fuels. Each Voluntary Project Activity (VPA) under this PoA will involve the manufacture of briquettes using agricultural residues and other organic biomass waste, which are typically discarded or left to decompose, resulting in methane emissions and environmental degradation. By converting this waste into high-density fuel briquettes, the PoA addresses key environmental and economic challenges. It contributes to greenhouse gas emission reductions by displacing fossil fuels and preventing methane emissions from un-managed biomass waste. The initiative also supports improved waste management through the productive use of agricultural residues, offers access to cleaner-burning fuels for small and medium-sized industrial units, and generates local employment across the biomass value chain—from raw material collection and processing to transportation and distribution. Additionally,by reducing the use of coal and wood, the PoA helps improve air quality and public health through lower emissions of particulate matter and other harmful pollutants.

column2: BIWACALI
column165:
BIWACALI stands for Burka Initiative for Water Balancing, Carbon Sequestration and Livelihood Improvement. The Oromo word "Burquaa" means "burbling spring", symbolizing the main objective of this project: ensuring the water security of the West-Ethiopian Upper Dabana - and the East-Ethiopian Hakim Gara watersheds by restoring about 10,000 ha areas degraded area into forest over the next decades. This will be achieved by tree planting and applying the Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) technique, which is designed to significantly improve the income and livelihoods of local farming communities. 

Next to the physical restoration work, major project activities are the formation of cooperatives and unions for forest management and training on FMNR, sustainable farming methods and alternative livelihoods. The newly created cooperatives will be strongly supported by World Vision Ethiopia in the first years of the project. It is envisioned that afterwards, they will take on the main responsibility for managing the forest areas, their products and the monitoring of the project impacts. 

The project is being implemented jointly by the local communities, Heineken Ethiopia, World Vision Ethiopia and FORLIANCE.

column2: FS BECCS Project
column165:
The FS BECCS project, proposed under the Gold Standard for Global Goals (GS4GG), reflects FS – Fueling Sustainability's ambition to lead Brazil's energy transition with innovation, technical excellence, and private investment. Founded in 2017, FS is the third-largest ethanol producer in the country, operating modern plants in Mato Grosso.

At its Lucas do Rio Verde facility, FS will capture biogenic CO₂ from corn ethanol fermentation. The stream, with about 98% purity, will be compressed, dehydrated, and injected into deep geological formations of the Parecis Basin for secure, long-term storage. As this CO₂ originates from the atmosphere via photosynthesis, its storage delivers net carbon removals.

Project development followed four phases: Phase 1 (2019–2020) confirmed storage potential through feasibility studies and 2D seismic data. Phase 2 (2020–2022) added a 3D seismic survey and design of capture and compression systems. Phase 3 (2022–2024) drilled a stratigraphic well, collected geological data, and began equipment procurement. Phase 4 (2024–2026), now underway, includes injectivity tests, well conversion, monitoring infrastructure, and capture system construction. Commercial operations are expected in 2025, with carbon injection June 2026.
